# Stocks matched by market beta

Daily closing prices, 2000 to 2026-10-30, from Yahoo Finance (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=False`).
Prices are **split-adjusted but not dividend-adjusted**, the same as the S&P 500 and
Nasdaq-100 index files, so all returns are measured the same way.

`market_beta.csv` lists each stock's market beta: the slope of its daily log return
against the S&P 500's (2005-2025). A beta of 1 means the stock moves about 1% when the
market moves 1%. The 20 stocks were chosen from about 80 large companies with full
price history since 2000, keeping those with beta between 0.9 and 1.1.

Caveat (beta window): the betas are measured over 2005-2025, a narrower window than
the data (2000-2026). Over the whole file several fall outside 0.9-1.1 (TXN 1.23,
CSCO 1.20, ORCL 1.20, AAPL 1.15, CVX 0.87, CI 0.90, TRV 0.90): the dot-com years
made some technology stocks move more than the market.

Caveat (survivorship bias): the candidates are companies that are large today, so
firms that failed or shrank since 2000 are missing.

from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

END = "2026-10-30"                  # last trading day included (a Friday)
INDEXES = {                         # file: (ticker, first day)
    "sp500_daily.csv": ("^GSPC", "1950-01-01"),
    "sp500_daily_from_1928.csv": ("^GSPC", "1927-12-01"),
    "nasdaq100_daily.csv": ("^NDX", "1985-10-01"),
    "vix_fear_index_daily.csv": ("^VIX", "1990-01-01"),
}
STOCK_START = "2000-01-01"
FRED_URL = "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=USREC"
DOW_URL = "https://www.measuringworth.com/datasets/DJA/result.php"
DOW_START = "1896-05-26"             # the first day of the Dow Jones Industrial Average


def daily_closes(ticker, start, end=END):
    """Daily closes from Yahoo as a DataFrame with a Date index and a Close column."""
    import yfinance as yf
    end_exclusive = (pd.Timestamp(end) + pd.Timedelta(days=1)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    df = yf.download(ticker, start=start, end=end_exclusive, auto_adjust=False,
                     progress=False, actions=False)
    if df.empty:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Yahoo returned no data for {ticker}")
    close = df["Close"]
    if isinstance(close, pd.DataFrame):          # newer yfinance: one column per ticker
        close = close.iloc[:, 0]
    out = close.dropna().rename("Close").to_frame()
    out.index = pd.to_datetime(out.index).tz_localize(None).normalize()
    out.index.name = "Date"
    return out


def recessions(end=END):
    """NBER recession indicator by month (1 = recession) from FRED, up to END."""
    import ssl
    import certifi                       # trusted certificates (installed with yfinance)
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=certifi.where())
    with urllib.request.urlopen(FRED_URL, timeout=30, context=ctx) as resp:

def dow_jones(first=1927, last=1952):
    """Daily Dow closes from MeasuringWorth (its query form returns an HTML table)."""
    import html
    import re
    from urllib.parse import urlencode
    form = urlencode(dict(monthStartD=1, dayStartD=1, yearStartD=first,
                          monthEndD=12, dayEndD=31, yearEndD=last)).encode()
    page = _fetch(DOW_URL, data=form)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", page)).replace("\xa0", " "))
    rows = re.findall(r"\b(\d{1,2})/(\d{1,2})/(\d{4}) ([\d.]+)", text)
    df = pd.DataFrame({"Date": pd.to_datetime([f"{y}-{m}-{d}" for m, d, y, _ in rows]),
                       "Close": [float(c) for *_, c in rows]}).drop_duplicates("Date")
    return df[(df["Date"].dt.year >= first) & (df["Date"].dt.year <= last)].set_index("Date")

def dow_jones(first=1927, last=1952):
    """Daily Dow closes from MeasuringWorth (its query form returns an HTML table)."""
    import html
    import re
    from urllib.parse import urlencode
    form = urlencode(dict(monthStartD=1, dayStartD=1, yearStartD=first,
                          monthEndD=12, dayEndD=31, yearEndD=last)).encode()
    page = _fetch(DOW_URL, data=form)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", page)).replace("\xa0", " "))
    rows = re.findall(r"\b(\d{1,2})/(\d{1,2})/(\d{4}) ([\d.]+)", text)
    df = pd.DataFrame({"Date": pd.to_datetime([f"{y}-{m}-{d}" for m, d, y, _ in rows]),
                       "Close": [float(c) for *_, c in rows]}).drop_duplicates("Date")
    return df[(df["Date"].dt.year >= first) & (df["Date"].dt.year <= last)].set_index("Date")

"""Outside factors (extension): news that every trader sees at the same moment.

Lux & Marchesi model news as small bell-curve steps in the value. Some real news is
different: an oil shock, a jump in interest rates or a Fed decision reaches every trader
at once, and a fully logical trader acts on it with no herding at all. If such news
carried the S&P 500's fat tails and volatility clustering, herding would not be needed to
explain them. This module measures how much it carries.

Data (data/download_market_data.py; every series ends 2026-10-30):
    oil     Brent crude oil, $/barrel (FRED DCOILBRENTEU, 1987-)
    gold    gold futures, front month (Yahoo GC=F, 2000-)
    copper  copper futures, front month (Yahoo HG=F, 2000-)
    dollar  broad trade-weighted US dollar (FRED DTWEXBGS, 2006-)
    rates   10-year Treasury yield (FRED DGS10, 1962-); its daily change in percentage
            points, since a yield is already a rate (a log change of a rate means little)
    data/fed_decisions.csv: FOMC decision days since February 1994 (scheduled meetings and
            the 9 surprise moves between meetings)

Timing: commodity futures settle in the early afternoon (gold 1:30 pm, oil 2:30 pm New York
time), the S&P closes at 4 pm. A late S&P move therefore shows up in the next day's commodity
change. Following Dimson (1979, J. Financial Economics 7, 197-226) the regressions include
each factor's change on the day before and the day after as well as the same day.
"""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from . import market_data, stats
from .checks import finite_1d

FACTOR_DIR = market_data.DATA / "factors"
FACTORS = {"oil": "oil_brent.csv", "gold": "gold.csv", "copper": "copper.csv",
           "dollar": "dollar_index.csv", "rates": "treasury_10y_yield.csv"}
LEVEL_CHANGE = {"rates"}                 # measured as a difference, not a log change
FED = market_data.DATA / "fed_decisions.csv"


def changes(name):
    """Daily changes of one outside factor, as a Series indexed by the later date: log
    changes of prices, and percentage-point changes of the 10-year yield."""
    if name not in FACTORS:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown factor {name!r}; choose from {sorted(FACTORS)}")
    level = market_data.load_prices(FACTOR_DIR / FACTORS[name])["Close"]
    out = level.diff() if name in LEVEL_CHANGE else np.log(level).diff()
    return out.dropna().rename(name)


def table(r, names):
    """The S&P's returns (column 'spx') next to the factors' changes, on the days when
    every one of them has a value. A factor that did not trade on an S&P day (a commodity
    holiday) drops that day; its change on the next day spans both days."""
    if len(names) == 0:
        raise ValueError("need at least one factor")
    df = pd.concat([pd.Series(r, name="spx")] + [changes(n) for n in names], axis=1, join="inner")
    if len(df) < 500:
        raise ValueError(f"only {len(df)} days in common; need at least 500")
    return df


def with_leads_lags(df, names, lags=1):
    """The columns `names` shifted by -lags..+lags days (Dimson 1979), as a new frame
    named like 'oil[+1]' (tomorrow's oil change). Rows with a missing shift are dropped."""
    if isinstance(lags, bool) or int(lags) != lags or lags < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"lags must be a whole number >= 0, got {lags}")
    cols = {f"{n}[{k:+d}]": df[n].shift(-k) for n in names for k in range(-int(lags), int(lags) + 1)}
    return pd.DataFrame(cols, index=df.index).dropna()


def regress(y, X):
    """Least squares of y on the columns of X with an intercept: (betas, intercept, R^2,
    residuals). R^2 = share of y's variance the columns explain."""
    y = finite_1d(y, "y")
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    if X.ndim == 1:
        X = X[:, None]
    if X.ndim != 2 or len(X) != len(y):

def r2_by_regime(r, names, window=20, lags=1):
    """R^2 of the factor regression in calm, middle and wild markets: days are split into
    thirds by the S&P's volatility over the `window` days before (known in advance, so no
    look-ahead). Herding predicts a lower R^2 in wild markets, where traders' own dynamics
    add moves that no outside news explains. Returns {'calm': R^2, 'middle': ..., 'wild': ...}."""
    df = table(r, names)
    X = with_leads_lags(df, names, lags)
    vol = df["spx"].rolling(int(window)).std().shift(1).loc[X.index]
    keep = vol.notna()
    X, vol, y = X[keep], vol[keep], df["spx"].loc[X.index[keep]]
    third = pd.qcut(vol, 3, labels=["calm", "middle", "wild"])
    return {k: regress(y[third == k].values, X[third == k].values)[2] for k in ("calm", "middle", "wild")}

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.325/27faf9f71f1d22a6ddb5ba5f703c402f/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
   One exception to direct name labels: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
  One exception, legend kept: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical, except that dark-mode good is the series green |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

    z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
    keep = z > 0
    z, cc = z[keep], cc[keep]
    if points:
        grid = np.geomspace(z[0], z[-1], points)
        i = np.unique(np.append(np.minimum(np.searchsorted(z, grid), len(z) - 1), len(z) - 1))
        z, cc = z[i], cc[i]
        kw = dict(dict(ls="none", marker="o", ms=4), **kw)
    ax.loglog(z, cc, color=color, label=label, **kw)


def gaussian_ccdf(ax, label="bell curve N(0,1)", ls="--"):
    g = np.geomspace(0.05, 6, 200)
    # share of a bell curve beyond +-x: erfc(x / sqrt 2). (math.erfc, not scipy: scipy
    # takes about half a second to load, in every worker process)
    ax.loglog(g, [erfc(x / np.sqrt(2)) for x in g], ls, color=MUTED, lw=1.2, label=label)


def power_law(ax, x0, y0, slope, x1, label=None, color=MUTED, **kw):
    """Reference line y = y0 (x / x0)^slope from x0 to x1: a straight line of the given
    slope on log-log axes (a tail exponent is minus the slope; H is the slope)."""
    x = np.array([x0, x1])
    return ax.loglog(x, y0 * (x / x0) ** slope, color=color, label=label, **dict(dict(ls="--", lw=1.1), **kw))[0]


def dfa(ax, x, scales, label, color, marker="o", shift=1.0, fit_ls="-"):
    """DFA fluctuation F(n) vs window n (log-log), with the fitted slope H in the label.
    Returns (H, the first window, its fitted F) so a reference slope can start there."""
    s, F = stats.dfa(x, scales)
    coef = np.polyfit(np.log(s), np.log(F), 1)
    ax.loglog(s, F * shift, marker, color=color, ms=4.5, lw=0, label=f"{label}: H = {coef[0]:.2f}")
    fit = np.exp(np.polyval(coef, np.log(s))) * shift
    ax.loglog(s, fit, fit_ls, color=color, lw=1.0)
    return coef[0], s[0], fit[0]


def comparison(real, model_r, z, no_chartists, path):
    """main.py's quick 2x2 overview: S&P vs model returns, tails, chartist share."""
    style()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5))
    n = min(len(real), len(model_r))
    for a, r, c, name in [(ax[0, 0], real[-n:], REAL, "S&P 500"),
                          (ax[0, 1], model_r[-n:], SPX_MODEL, "model (S&P-calibrated)")]:
        a.plot(stats.standardize(r), lw=0.35, color=c)
        a.set_ylim(-25, 25)
        a.set_title(f"{name}: daily returns ({n:,} days)")
        a.set_ylabel("return / standard deviation")
    a = ax[1, 0]
    ccdf(a, real, "S&P 500", REAL)
    ccdf(a, model_r, "model", SPX_MODEL)
    ccdf(a, no_chartists, "model, no chartists", NEWS)

    g = np.geomspace(0.05, 6, 200)

def power_law(ax, x0, y0, slope, x1, label=None, color=MUTED, **kw):
    """Reference line y = y0 (x / x0)^slope from x0 to x1: a straight line of the given
    slope on log-log axes (a tail exponent is minus the slope; H is the slope)."""
    x = np.array([x0, x1])
    return ax.loglog(x, y0 * (x / x0) ** slope, color=color, label=label, **dict(dict(ls="--", lw=1.1), **kw))[0]


def dfa(ax, x, scales, label, color, marker="o", shift=1.0, fit_ls="-"):
    """DFA fluctuation F(n) vs window n (log-log), with the fitted slope H in the label.
    Returns (H, the first window, its fitted F) so a reference slope can start there."""
    s, F = stats.dfa(x, scales)
    coef = np.polyfit(np.log(s), np.log(F), 1)
    ax.loglog(s, F * shift, marker, color=color, ms=4.5, lw=0, label=f"{label}: H = {coef[0]:.2f}")
    fit = np.exp(np.polyval(coef, np.log(s))) * shift
    ax.loglog(s, fit, fit_ls, color=color, lw=1.0)
    return coef[0], s[0], fit[0]

               f"{resid.index[0]:%Y}-{resid.index[-1]:%Y} ({len(resid):,} days). 'Outside news removed': the S&P's "
               f"daily returns minus the part explained by oil, gold, copper and the 10-year interest rate on the "
               "day before, the day itself and the day after. This removes too much rather than too little, because "
               "part of what moves with those markets is the stock market's own panic.\nIn b each dot is the "
               "S&P's percentile among held-out histories of the S&P-calibrated model of the same length. "
               "Surprise Fed moves are huge days, but there are only 9; scheduled decisions are ordinary days.")
    return dict(r2=r2, days=len(resid), raw=fp_raw, resid=fp_res, pct_raw=pct_raw, pct_res=pct_res,
                histories=len(sims), fed=fed)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Fig 18
def fig18_moments(spx, pool, path=FIG / "fig18_trading_moments_with_error_bars.png"):
    """Mean, spread, skewness and kurtosis of the S&P with 95% block-bootstrap intervals,
    against the same four numbers in model histories of the same length."""
    m = stats.moments(spx.values)
    runs = model_runs(len(spx), pool=pool)
    sims = {k: np.array([f(r) for r in runs]) for k, f in
            (("mean", np.mean), ("sd", np.std), ("skew", stats.skewness), ("kurtosis", stats.kurtosis))}
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.8))
    pct = {}
    scale = {"mean": 1e4, "sd": 100, "skew": 1, "kurtosis": 1}
    unit = {"mean": "basis points a day", "sd": "% a day", "skew": "", "kurtosis": ""}
    for a, k in zip(ax, stats.MOMENTS):
        v, lo, hi = (x * scale[k] for x in m[k])
        s = sims[k] * scale[k]
        pct[k] = experiments.percentile(m[k][0], sims[k])
        jitter = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(-1, 1, len(s))
        a.plot(s, jitter, "o", color=SPX_MODEL, ms=4, alpha=0.7, label="model histories")
        a.axvspan(lo, hi, color=REAL, alpha=0.12, lw=0, label="S&P 95% interval")
        a.axvline(v, color=REAL, lw=2, label="S&P 500")
        if k == "kurtosis":
            a.set_xscale("symlog", linthresh=1)
        a.set_yticks([])
        a.set_ylim(-1.6, 1.6)
        a.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
        a.set_xlabel(unit[k])
        a.set_title(f"{k}: S&P {v:.2f} ({lo:.2f} to {hi:.2f})\nat {pct[k]:.0f}% of the model", loc="left",
                    fontsize=9.5)
    ax[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.12, 1, 0.9))
    plots.save(fig, path, "Fig 18. The four trading moments, with error bars: the model is symmetric, the S&P is not",
               f"S&P 500, {spx.index[0]:%Y}-{spx.index[-1]:%Y}. Shaded: 95% interval from a block bootstrap (resampled "
               "one-year blocks, so wild spells stay together). Dots: held-out histories of the S&P-calibrated model, "
               "same length. The S&P falls harder than it rises (negative skew); the model's traders behave the "
               "same in both directions. The kurtosis interval is very wide: one day (Black Monday) dominates it.")
    return dict(moments=m, percentile=pct, histories=len(runs))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ all
def main():
    plots.style()
    spx = market_data.spx_returns()
    with Pool() as pool:
        out = dict(fig16=fig16_comovement(spx), fig17=fig17_without_outside_news(spx, pool),
                   fig18=fig18_moments(spx, pool))
    f17 = out["fig17"]
    print(f"Outside news explains {f17['r2']:.1%} of the S&P's daily variance ({f17['days']:,} days)")
    print(f"{'measure':<22}{'S&P':>8}{'removed':>9}{'pct':>6}{'pct rm':>8}")
    for k in SCALE_FREE:
        print(f"{SHORT[k]:<22}{f17['raw'][k]:8.3f}{f17['resid'][k]:9.3f}{f17['pct_raw'][k]:6.0f}{f17['pct_res'][k]:8.0f}")
    for k, v in f17["fed"].items():
        print(f"Fed {k}: {v}")
    print("R^2 by regime:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in out["fig16"]["regimes"].items()})
    print("moments:", out["fig18"]["moments"], out["fig18"]["percentile"])
    print("saved fig16, fig17, fig18 in", FIG)
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Outside news (extension): commodities, interest rates, the dollar and the Fed
(figures/fig16-fig18*.png), and the numbers behind them.

Run:  python3 scripts/outside_news_figures.py        (about half a minute on 8 cores)

    fig16  how the S&P 500 moves with oil, gold, copper, the dollar and interest rates
    fig17  take out what outside news explains: do the fat tails and memory survive?
    fig18  the four trading moments of the S&P 500, with error bars, against the model

The question (see herding/factors.py): some news reaches every trader at once and a
logical trader acts on it with no herding at all. Does such news, rather than herding,
make the S&P's fat tails and volatility clustering?
Every number printed on a figure is computed here from the data, never typed in.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))   # the project folder, so `herding` imports

from multiprocessing import Pool

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from herding import calibrate, experiments, factors, market_data, plots, stats
from herding.plots import BLUE, INK, MUTED, ORANGE, REAL, SECOND, SPX_MODEL, plt

FIG = market_data.ROOT / "figures"
ALL = ("oil", "gold", "copper", "dollar", "rates")
NAMES = {"oil": "oil (Brent)", "gold": "gold", "copper": "copper", "dollar": "US dollar",
         "rates": "10-year interest rate"}
WINDOW = ("oil", "gold", "copper", "rates")      # 2000-: longer than with the dollar (2006-)
SEEDS = calibrate.HELD_OUT_SEEDS[:40]
SCALE_FREE = ("kurtosis", "alpha_hill", "alpha_reg", "ac_abs_1", "ac_abs_50", "H_abs", "kurt_5", "kurt_25")
SHORT = {"kurtosis": "kurtosis", "alpha_hill": "tail α (Hill)", "alpha_reg": "tail α (paper's way)",
         "ac_abs_1": "clustering, next day", "ac_abs_50": "clustering, 50 days", "H_abs": "memory H of |r|",
         "kurt_5": "kurtosis, 5 days", "kurt_25": "kurtosis, 25 days"}
CORR_FACTORS = ("oil", "rates", "gold")          # the rolling-correlation panels


def model_runs(days, seeds=SEEDS, pool=None):
    """Held-out histories of the S&P-calibrated model, `days` long; runaways are dropped
    (and counted by the caller from the length)."""
    out = experiments.histories(calibrate.load("spx"), seeds, days, pool=pool)
    return [h["r"] for h in out if h is not None]


def percentiles(value_fp, sims):
    """The percentile of each scale-free measure of `value_fp` among the model histories."""
    return {k: experiments.percentile(value_fp[k], np.array([f[k] for f in sims])) for k in SCALE_FREE}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Fig 16
def fig16_comovement(spx, path=FIG / "fig16_sp500_with_commodities_and_rates.png"):
    """Correlations (all days vs crash days), rolling correlations, and the share of S&P
    moves the outside factors explain in calm and wild markets."""
    b = factors.betas(spx, ALL)
    crash = {n: factors.crash_corr(spx, factors.changes(n)) for n in ALL}
    regimes = factors.r2_by_regime(spx, ALL)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15, 9))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 3, height_ratios=(1, 1), hspace=0.42, wspace=0.28)

    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    y = np.arange(len(ALL))
    a.barh(y + 0.2, [crash[n][1] for n in ALL], 0.38, color=MUTED, label="other days")
    a.barh(y - 0.2, [crash[n][0] for n in ALL], 0.38, color=INK, label="the S&P's worst 5% of days")
    a.set_yticks(y, [NAMES[n] for n in ALL])
    a.invert_yaxis()
    a.axvline(0, color=SECOND, lw=0.9)
    a.set_xlabel("correlation with the S&P 500 (same day)")
    a.set_title("a. Moving together, and in crashes", loc="left")
    a.legend(loc="lower right")
    a.grid(axis="y", visible=False)

    for i, n in enumerate(CORR_FACTORS):
        a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1 + i] if i < 2 else gs[1, 0])
        rc = factors.rolling_corr(spx, factors.changes(n))
        a.axhline(0, color=SECOND, lw=0.9)
        a.fill_between(rc.index, 0, rc.values, where=rc.values >= 0, color=BLUE, alpha=0.25, lw=0, interpolate=True)
        a.fill_between(rc.index, 0, rc.values, where=rc.values <= 0, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.3, lw=0, interpolate=True)
        a.plot(rc.index, rc.values, color=INK, lw=1)
        a.set_ylim(-0.8, 0.8)
        a.set_ylabel("1-year correlation")
        flips = int((np.diff(np.sign(rc.values)) != 0).sum())
        a.set_title(f"{'bcd'[i]}. S&P with {NAMES[n]}: the sign changed {flips} times", loc="left")

    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])
    keys = ("calm", "middle", "wild")
    bars = a.bar(keys, [100 * regimes[k] for k in keys], color=[MUTED, SECOND, INK], width=0.6)
    a.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.0f%%", color=INK, fontsize=9)
    a.set_ylabel("share of the S&P's daily variance explained")
    a.set_xlabel("market, by its volatility over the 20 days before")
    a.set_title("e. Outside markets explain more in wild times", loc="left")
    a.yaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0f}%")
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)

    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2])
    a.axis("off")
    rows = [f"{NAMES[n]:<22}{b[n]['corr']:+.2f}   {b[n]['spx_beta']:+.2f}" for n in ALL]
    a.text(0, 1, "f. One number per factor (2006-2026)\n\n" + f"{'':<22}corr    S&P beta\n" + "\n".join(rows)
           + "\n\nS&P beta: the S&P's move per 1 unit of\nthe factor's move (per 1 point of yield\n"
             "for rates, per 1% for the others).",
           family="DejaVu Sans Mono", fontsize=9, va="top", color=INK)
    plots.save(fig, path, "Fig 16. Commodities, interest rates and the dollar: how the S&P 500 moves with them",
               "Daily changes on days all markets traded (2006-2026 for a, e, f; each factor's own full history in "
               "b-d). Copper and oil rise with stocks; the dollar falls when stocks rise; gold hardly moves with "
               "them, even in crashes (a 'safe haven', Baur & Lucey 2010). The stock-oil and stock-interest-rate "
               "links changed sign over the years, so no fixed beta describes them.\nIn e, the factors (each on the "
               "day before, the day itself and the day after; Dimson 1979) explain more of the S&P's moves in wild "
               "markets. That does not mean news causes the crashes: in a panic the S&P also moves oil and rates.")
    return dict(betas=b, crash=crash, regimes=regimes)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Fig 17
def fig17_without_outside_news(spx, pool, path=FIG / "fig17_without_outside_news.png"):
    """Remove every move the factors explain, and Fed decision days: are the fat tails and
    the memory still there, and is the S&P still a typical model history?"""
    resid, r2 = factors.remove(spx, WINDOW)
    raw = spx.loc[resid.index]
    sims = [stats.fingerprint(r) for r in model_runs(len(resid), pool=pool)]
    fp_raw, fp_res = stats.fingerprint(raw.values), stats.fingerprint(resid.values)
    pct_raw, pct_res = percentiles(fp_raw, sims), percentiles(fp_res, sims)
    since94 = spx[spx.index >= "1994-02-01"]
    fed = {k: factors.event_days(since94, factors.on_days(since94.index, factors.decisions(k)["date"]))
           for k in ("scheduled", "unscheduled")}
    fed["all"] = factors.event_days(since94, factors.on_days(since94.index, factors.decisions()["date"]))

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8.5))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 3, width_ratios=(1, 1.25, 1), hspace=0.45, wspace=0.3)
    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 0])
    plots.ccdf(a, raw.values, "S&P 500", REAL, points=40)
    plots.ccdf(a, resid.values, "S&P with outside news removed", REAL, points=40, mfc="white")
    plots.gaussian_ccdf(a)
    a.set_xlim(0.3, 20)
    a.set_ylim(1e-4, 1.2)
    a.set_xlabel("|return| / standard deviation")
    a.set_ylabel("share of days with a bigger move")
    a.set_title(f"a. Outside news explains {r2:.0%} of the\nS&P's daily variance; the tail stays fat", loc="left")
    a.legend(loc="lower left")

    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 1])
    y = np.arange(len(SCALE_FREE))
    a.axvspan(5, 95, color=SPX_MODEL, alpha=0.1, lw=0)
    for k, yy in zip(SCALE_FREE, y):
        a.plot([pct_raw[k], pct_res[k]], [yy, yy], color=MUTED, lw=1, zorder=1)
    a.plot([pct_raw[k] for k in SCALE_FREE], y, "o", color=REAL, ms=8, label="S&P 500", zorder=2)
    a.plot([pct_res[k] for k in SCALE_FREE], y, "o", color=REAL, mfc="white", ms=8,
           label="outside news removed", zorder=3)
    a.set_yticks(y, [SHORT[k] for k in SCALE_FREE])
    a.invert_yaxis()
    a.set_xlim(-3, 103)
    a.set_xlabel(f"percentile among {len(sims)} model histories (blue band: typical, 5-95%)")
    ok = (sum(5 <= pct_raw[k] <= 95 for k in SCALE_FREE), sum(5 <= pct_res[k] <= 95 for k in SCALE_FREE))
    a.set_title(f"b. Still a typical history of the herding model?\n"
                f"typical on {ok[0]} of {len(SCALE_FREE)} measures, then {ok[1]} of {len(SCALE_FREE)}", loc="left")
    a.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8.5)
    a.grid(axis="y", visible=False)

    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    kinds = ("scheduled", "unscheduled")
    bars = a.bar([f"scheduled\n({fed['scheduled']['days']} days)", f"surprise\n({fed['unscheduled']['days']} days)"],
                 [fed[k]["size_ratio"] for k in kinds], color=[MUTED, INK], width=0.55)
    a.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.1f×", color=INK, fontsize=9)
    a.axhline(1, color=SECOND, lw=0.9, ls="--")
    a.set_ylabel("move size vs. other days")
    a.set_title("c. Fed decision days, 1994-2026", loc="left")
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)

    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2])
    a.axis("off")
    f = fed["all"]
    a.text(0, 1, f"d. Leaving out all {f['days']} Fed days\n\n"
                 f"{'':<16}with   without\n"
                 f"{'kurtosis':<16}{f['kurtosis_all']:5.1f}   {f['kurtosis_without']:5.1f}\n"
                 f"{'tail α (Hill)':<16}{f['alpha_all']:5.2f}   {f['alpha_without']:5.2f}\n\n"
                 f"They are {f['chance_share']:.0%} of days and {f['big_share']:.0%}\nof the biggest 1% of days.",
           family="DejaVu Sans Mono", fontsize=9.5, va="top", color=INK)
    plots.save(fig, path, "Fig 17. Take out the outside news: the fat tails and the memory survive",
               f"{resid.index[0]:%Y}-{resid.index[-1]:%Y} ({len(resid):,} days). 'Outside news removed': the S&P's "
               f"daily returns minus the part explained by oil, gold, copper and the 10-year interest rate on the "
               "day before, the day itself and the day after. This removes too much rather than too little, because "
               "part of what moves with those markets is the stock market's own panic.\nIn b each dot is the "
               "S&P's percentile among held-out histories of the S&P-calibrated model of the same length. "
               "Surprise Fed moves are huge days, but there are only 9; scheduled decisions are ordinary days.")
    return dict(r2=r2, days=len(resid), raw=fp_raw, resid=fp_res, pct_raw=pct_raw, pct_res=pct_res,
                histories=len(sims), fed=fed)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Fig 18
def fig18_moments(spx, pool, path=FIG / "fig18_trading_moments_with_error_bars.png"):
    """Mean, spread, skewness and kurtosis of the S&P with 95% block-bootstrap intervals,
    against the same four numbers in model histories of the same length."""
    m = stats.moments(spx.values)
    runs = model_runs(len(spx), pool=pool)
    sims = {k: np.array([f(r) for r in runs]) for k, f in
            (("mean", np.mean), ("sd", np.std), ("skew", stats.skewness), ("kurtosis", stats.kurtosis))}
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.8))
    pct = {}
    scale = {"mean": 1e4, "sd": 100, "skew": 1, "kurtosis": 1}
    unit = {"mean": "basis points a day", "sd": "% a day", "skew": "", "kurtosis": ""}
    for a, k in zip(ax, stats.MOMENTS):
        v, lo, hi = (x * scale[k] for x in m[k])
        s = sims[k] * scale[k]
        pct[k] = experiments.percentile(m[k][0], sims[k])
        jitter = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(-1, 1, len(s))
        a.plot(s, jitter, "o", color=SPX_MODEL, ms=4, alpha=0.7, label="model histories")
        a.axvspan(lo, hi, color=REAL, alpha=0.12, lw=0, label="S&P 95% interval")
        a.axvline(v, color=REAL, lw=2, label="S&P 500")
        if k == "kurtosis":
            a.set_xscale("symlog", linthresh=1)
        a.set_yticks([])
        a.set_ylim(-1.6, 1.6)
        a.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
        a.set_xlabel(unit[k])
        a.set_title(f"{k}: S&P {v:.2f} ({lo:.2f} to {hi:.2f})\nat {pct[k]:.0f}% of the model", loc="left",
                    fontsize=9.5)
    ax[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.12, 1, 0.9))
    plots.save(fig, path, "Fig 18. The four trading moments, with error bars: the model is symmetric, the S&P is not",
               f"S&P 500, {spx.index[0]:%Y}-{spx.index[-1]:%Y}. Shaded: 95% interval from a block bootstrap (resampled "
               "one-year blocks, so wild spells stay together). Dots: held-out histories of the S&P-calibrated model, "
               "same length. The S&P falls harder than it rises (negative skew); the model's traders behave the "
               "same in both directions. The kurtosis interval is very wide: one day (Black Monday) dominates it.")
    return dict(moments=m, percentile=pct, histories=len(runs))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ all
def main():
    plots.style()
    spx = market_data.spx_returns()
    with Pool() as pool:
        out = dict(fig16=fig16_comovement(spx), fig17=fig17_without_outside_news(spx, pool),
                   fig18=fig18_moments(spx, pool))
    f17 = out["fig17"]
    print(f"Outside news explains {f17['r2']:.1%} of the S&P's daily variance ({f17['days']:,} days)")
    print(f"{'measure':<22}{'S&P':>8}{'removed':>9}{'pct':>6}{'pct rm':>8}")
    for k in SCALE_FREE:
        print(f"{SHORT[k]:<22}{f17['raw'][k]:8.3f}{f17['resid'][k]:9.3f}{f17['pct_raw'][k]:6.0f}{f17['pct_res'][k]:8.0f}")
    for k, v in f17["fed"].items():
        print(f"Fed {k}: {v}")
    print("R^2 by regime:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in out["fig16"]["regimes"].items()})
    print("moments:", out["fig18"]["moments"], out["fig18"]["percentile"])
    print("saved fig16, fig17, fig18 in", FIG)
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":

# Test every function

## What this skill does
It flips the AI from "make it run" to "prove it is right." When it is on, the AI does not consider a function done until it has said what success means, written tests that cover the ordinary case and the edges, and shown you the tests so you can judge them. You stay the manager who owns "done."

## The rule you are enforcing
Karpathy's line: today's AI automates what you can **verify**. So the skill is not writing tests by hand, it is telling the AI what counts as success and demanding every function be tested against it. The bar for every function: **would you bet a million dollars this is right?** If not, it is not tested enough.

## How to respond when this skill is active
1. **Specify success first.** Before testing a function, state in one plain sentence what it must do and how you will know it worked. If the spec is vague, ask the user to sharpen it. A vague ask gets a confident wrong answer.
2. **Test every function on its own.** Break the work into small functions and check each one. Checking that the whole program runs is not the same as checking each piece is correct.
3. **Hit the edges as well as the happy path.** For each function, enumerate: the ordinary case, the empty/zero/one case, the boundary case, and the case the spec is silent on. Write a test for each.
4. **Name the silent-failure trap.** A function that returns a hardcoded answer for the one input you tested will pass that test and still be wrong. So test more than one input, and test inputs whose answer you can compute independently.
5. **Show the tests and the reasoning.** Print the tests and say what each one is checking, so the human can confirm the coverage. Do not hide verification inside "looks good."
6. **Verify without a human where you can.** Prefer checks the code can run itself (assert expected == actual) over "eyeball the output." If a check truly needs human judgment, say so and keep the human in the loop for that one.
7. **Report honestly.** End with: which functions are covered, which edges are tested, and where you would NOT yet bet $1M. Do not declare done past that line.

## Good practice
- Plan top-down, test bottom-up: design the whole thing first, then verify the small pieces that make it up.
- One behavior per test, with a name that says what it checks.
- When a test fails, fix the code or the spec, then re-run; never delete a failing test to make it green.
- Testing is a craft. The goal is coverage of the ways this specific function can go wrong, rather than a fixed number of tests.

## Pitfalls
- Tests that only re-run the happy path give false confidence.
- Asserting on output you never independently computed just checks the code agrees with itself.
- "It compiles and runs" is the black-box gambler's standard. The manager's standard is "I can show you why it is right."

"""Tests for data.py and the downloaded data files.  Run: python3 -m pytest tests/ -q

Every test states what "correct" means, and uses inputs whose answer we know
independently (math or published facts), across several random seeds.
"""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from conftest import ROOT
from herding import market_data as data



# --------------------------------------------------------------- real data
# Spec: data files are clean and match known historical values.

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def spx():
    return pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/sp500_daily.csv", parse_dates=["Date"], index_col="Date")


def test_spx_clean(spx):
    assert spx.index.is_monotonic_increasing and not spx.index.duplicated().any()
    assert spx["Close"].notna().all() and (spx["Close"] > 0).all()


def test_every_file_ends_on_the_same_fixed_day():
    # The old files ended on different days, and their last row was a live
    # (mid-day) price, not the official close. data/download_market_data.py stops every
    # series at the same END date.
    import importlib.util
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("download", data.DATA / "download_market_data.py")
    download = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(download)
    end = data.pd.Timestamp(download.END)
    files = [data.DATA / name for name in download.INDEXES]
    files += [data.STOCKS / f"{t}.csv" for t in data.stock_tickers()]
    for f in files:
        assert data.load_prices(f).index[-1] == end, f.name
    months = data.pd.read_csv(data.DATA / "us_recessions_monthly.csv", parse_dates=[0])
    assert months.iloc[-1, 0] == end.to_period("M").to_timestamp()


# Audit of November 2026, issue 4: three broken files that used to slip through or give a
# confusing error (inf passed "> 0"; text gave TypeError; no Close column gave KeyError)
@pytest.mark.parametrize("body, words", [
    ("Date,Close\n2020-01-02,100\n2020-01-03,inf\n", "finite"),
    ("Date,Close\n2020-01-02,100\n2020-01-03,abc\n", "number"),
    ("Date,Price\n2020-01-02,100\n", "Close"),
    ("Close\n100\n", "Date")])
"""Tests for scripts/party_figures.py (Figs 13-15): every figure is drawn from small
made-up returns, and the numbers it reports agree with the same numbers computed here
in a different way (parties from hand-typed dates, plain numpy sums)."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest
from matplotlib.image import imread

import party_figures as pf
from herding import politics


def market(seed=0, start="1989-06-01", end="2012-12-31"):
    """Made-up daily log returns over Bush (R), Clinton (D), Bush (R), Obama (D)."""
    days = pd.bdate_range(start, end)
    return pd.Series(0.01 * np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_t(4, len(days)) + 0.0003, index=days)


def dem_by_hand(dates):
    """Democratic days from typed-in inauguration dates (not politics.democrat)."""
    d = pd.DatetimeIndex(dates)
    return ((d >= "1993-01-20") & (d < "2001-01-20")) | ((d >= "2009-01-20") & (d < "2017-01-20"))


def is_image(path):
    return path.exists() and imread(path).shape[0] > 200


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- small helpers
def test_years_between_counts_both_end_days():
    assert pf.years_between("2001-01-01", "2001-12-31") == pytest.approx(365 / 365.25)
    assert pf.years_between("2000-03-01", "2000-03-01") == pytest.approx(1 / 365.25)


def test_event_name_only_inside_the_windows():
    assert pf.event_name("1987-10-19") == "Black Monday"
    assert pf.event_name("1987-10-20") == ""               # one day late: no label
    assert pf.event_name("1929-10-28") == "1929 crash"
    assert pf.event_name("2008-10-15") == "2008 financial crisis"
    assert pf.event_name("2020-03-16") == "Covid panic"
"""Shared test setup: make the project importable, common seeds, slow marker."""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent

"""Tests for herding/factors.py, the outside-factor data files, the Fed decision days, and
scripts/outside_news_figures.py (Figs 16-18).

Every test states what "correct" means and checks it against an answer found another way:
made-up data with a known answer (an exact line, a mirror image), a property least squares
must have (residuals uncorrelated with every regressor), or a published historical fact.
"""
import importlib.util

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest
from matplotlib.image import imread

from conftest import ROOT, SEEDS
from herding import factors, market_data, stats


def downloader():
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("download", ROOT / "data/download_market_data.py")
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
    return mod


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def spx():
    return market_data.spx_returns()


# --------------------------------------------------------------- data files
# Spec: each file is clean, ends on the project's fixed day, and matches known history.

def test_factor_files_are_clean_and_end_on_the_fixed_day():
    end = pd.Timestamp(downloader().END)
    for name, f in factors.FACTORS.items():
        prices = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / f)        # checks sorted, unique, > 0
        assert prices.index[-1] <= end, name
        assert (end - prices.index[-1]).days <= 4, name                 # at most a long weekend early


def test_brent_known_prices():
    # EIA: Brent's record close was $143.95 on 2008-07-03; it fell to $9.12 on 2020-04-21
    brent = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "oil_brent.csv")["Close"]
    assert brent["2008-07-03"] == pytest.approx(143.95)
    assert brent.idxmax() == pd.Timestamp("2008-07-03")
    assert brent["2020-04-21"] == pytest.approx(9.12)


def test_ten_year_yield_known_values():
    # The 10-year yield's all-time high was 15.84% (1981-09-30); it fell 0.75 points the
    # day after Black Monday as money fled to bonds
    y = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "treasury_10y_yield.csv")["Close"]
    assert y.idxmax() == pd.Timestamp("1981-09-30") and y.max() == pytest.approx(15.84)
    assert factors.changes("rates")["1987-10-20"] == pytest.approx(-0.75)


def test_fed_target_known_moves():
    # Fed history: cut to a 0-0.25% range on 2008-12-16; to 0-0.25% again on 2020-03-15
    t = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "fed_funds_target.csv")["Close"]
    assert t["2008-12-15"] == pytest.approx(1.0) and t["2008-12-16"] == pytest.approx(0.25)
    assert t["2020-03-16"] == pytest.approx(0.25) and t["2020-03-13"] == pytest.approx(1.25)


# --------------------------------------------------------------- Fed decision days
def test_surprise_moves_are_exactly_the_feds_intermeeting_moves():
    # The Fed's moves between scheduled meetings since 1994 (federalreserve.gov, "Open market
    # operations" history), dated by announcement, typed in here by hand
    known = {"1994-04-18": 25, "1998-10-15": -25, "2001-01-03": -50, "2001-04-18": -50,
             "2001-09-17": -50, "2008-01-22": -75, "2008-10-08": -50, "2020-03-03": -50,
             "2020-03-15": -100}
    d = factors.decisions("unscheduled")
    assert dict(zip(d["date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"), d["change_bp"])) == known


def test_scheduled_meetings_known_decisions():
    d = factors.decisions("scheduled").set_index("date")["change_bp"]
    assert d["2008-12-16"] == -75             # 1.00% -> 0-0.25%
    assert d["2022-06-15"] == 75              # the first 0.75-point hike since 1994
    assert d["2023-09-20"] == 0               # a pause
    assert d["2006-01-31"] == 25


def test_scheduled_meetings_are_weekdays_and_about_eight_a_year():
    d = factors.decisions("scheduled")["date"]
    assert (d.dt.dayofweek < 5).all()
    per_year = d.groupby(d.dt.year).size()
    assert per_year.between(7, 9).all(), per_year[~per_year.between(7, 9)]
    assert d.is_unique


def test_every_target_change_is_assigned_to_exactly_one_decision():
    # The changes in the target series must add up to the changes in the decision file
    t = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "fed_funds_target.csv")["Close"]
    t = t[t.index >= "1994-01-01"]
    total = round((t.iloc[-1] - t.iloc[0]) * 100)
    assert factors.decisions()["change_bp"].sum() == total


def test_decisions_rejects_unknown_kind():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="kind"):
        factors.decisions("emergency")


# The rules that build fed_decisions.csv, on made-up targets and meetings
@pytest.fixture
def dm(monkeypatch):
    mod = downloader()
    monkeypatch.setattr(mod, "scheduled_fomc_days",
                        lambda: pd.DatetimeIndex(["2005-03-22", "2005-05-03", "2015-12-16", "2016-03-16"]))
    return mod


def target(changes):
    days = pd.bdate_range("2005-01-03", "2016-06-30")
    rate = pd.Series(1.0, index=days)
    for day, bp in changes:
        rate[rate.index >= day] += bp / 100
    return rate.rename("Close").to_frame()


def test_fed_decisions_same_day_change_before_2008(dm):
    d = dm.fed_decisions(target([("2005-03-22", 25)]))
    assert d.set_index("date").loc["2005-03-22", "change_bp"] == 25
    assert (d["kind"] == "unscheduled").sum() == 0


def test_fed_decisions_next_day_change_after_2008_belongs_to_the_meeting(dm):
    # Since 2008-12-16 a new range takes effect the day after the announcement
    d = dm.fed_decisions(target([("2015-12-17", 25)]))
    assert d.set_index("date").loc["2015-12-16", "change_bp"] == 25
    assert (d["kind"] == "unscheduled").sum() == 0


def test_fed_decisions_surprise_is_dated_by_its_announcement(dm):
    d = dm.fed_decisions(target([("2005-04-12", -50), ("2016-01-20", -25)]))
    s = d[d["kind"] == "unscheduled"].set_index("date")["change_bp"]
    assert s.to_dict() == {pd.Timestamp("2005-04-12"): -50, pd.Timestamp("2016-01-19"): -25}


def test_last_day_of_meeting_parsing():
    mod = downloader()
    assert mod._last_day("March", "17-18", 2026) == pd.Timestamp("2026-03-18")
    assert mod._last_day("Oct/Nov", "31-1", 2023) == pd.Timestamp("2023-11-01")
    assert mod._last_day("September", "20", 2005) == pd.Timestamp("2005-09-20")


# --------------------------------------------------------------- changes / table
def test_changes_are_log_changes_or_yield_differences():
    oil = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "oil_brent.csv")["Close"]
    assert factors.changes("oil")["2020-04-21"] == pytest.approx(np.log(9.12 / 17.36))
    y = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "treasury_10y_yield.csv")["Close"]
    assert factors.changes("rates").values == pytest.approx(np.diff(y.values))
    assert len(factors.changes("oil")) == len(oil) - 1


def test_changes_rejects_unknown_factor():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="unknown factor"):
        factors.changes("silver")


def test_table_keeps_only_days_every_series_has(spx):
    df = factors.table(spx, ["oil", "dollar"])
    assert not df.isna().any().any()
    assert df.index.isin(spx.index).all()
    assert df.index.isin(factors.changes("dollar").index).all()
    assert df.index[0] >= pd.Timestamp("2006-01-03")          # the dollar series starts in 2006


def test_table_needs_factors_and_enough_days(spx):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="at least one"):
        factors.table(spx, [])
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="500"):
        factors.table(spx.iloc[-300:], ["oil"])


# --------------------------------------------------------------- with_leads_lags
def test_leads_and_lags_shift_the_right_way():
    df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, 2, 3, 4, 5]}, index=pd.bdate_range("2020-01-06", periods=5))
    out = factors.with_leads_lags(df, ["x"], 1)
    assert list(out.columns) == ["x[-1]", "x[+0]", "x[+1]"]
    assert out["x[-1]"].tolist() == [1, 2, 3]       # yesterday
    assert out["x[+0]"].tolist() == [2, 3, 4]
    assert out["x[+1]"].tolist() == [3, 4, 5]       # tomorrow
    assert factors.with_leads_lags(df, ["x"], 0)["x[+0]"].tolist() == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("bad", [-1, 1.5, True])
def test_leads_and_lags_rejects_bad_lags(bad):
    df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, 2, 3]})
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="lags"):
        factors.with_leads_lags(df, ["x"], bad)


# --------------------------------------------------------------- regress
@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_regress_recovers_an_exact_line(seed):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = g.normal(size=(200, 2))
    beta, icept, r2, resid = factors.regress(2 + 3 * X[:, 0] - X[:, 1], X)
    assert beta == pytest.approx([3, -1]) and icept == pytest.approx(2)
    assert r2 == pytest.approx(1) and np.abs(resid).max() < 1e-10


@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_regress_r2_matches_the_signal_share(seed):
    # y = x + noise with equal variances: R^2 should be about 1/2
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = g.normal(size=200_000)
    _, _, r2, resid = factors.regress(x + g.normal(size=x.size), x)
    assert r2 == pytest.approx(0.5, abs=0.01)
    assert abs(np.corrcoef(resid, x)[0, 1]) < 1e-10          # least squares: residual _|_ regressor


def test_regress_rejects_bad_input():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="constant"):
        factors.regress(np.ones(10), np.arange(10.0))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="one row"):
        factors.regress(np.arange(10.0), np.arange(9.0))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="more rows"):
        factors.regress(np.arange(3.0), np.ones((3, 2)))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="NaN"):
        factors.regress(np.arange(5.0), np.array([1, 2, np.nan, 4, 5]))


# --------------------------------------------------------------- remove / betas
def test_remove_leaves_nothing_the_factors_can_explain(spx):
    names = ["oil", "rates"]
    resid, r2 = factors.remove(spx, names)
    X = factors.with_leads_lags(factors.table(spx, names), names).loc[resid.index]
    for col in X:
        assert abs(np.corrcoef(resid, X[col])[0, 1]) < 1e-8, col
    assert resid.mean() == pytest.approx(spx.loc[resid.index].mean())
    assert 0 < r2 < 1


def test_more_factors_never_explain_less(spx):
    # Nested least squares: adding regressors can only raise R^2 (on the same days)
    small = factors.regress(*_design(spx, ["oil", "gold", "copper", "dollar", "rates"], ["oil"]))[2]
    big = factors.regress(*_design(spx, ["oil", "gold", "copper", "dollar", "rates"]))[2]
    assert big >= small


def _design(spx, names, use=None):
    df = factors.table(spx, names)
    X = factors.with_leads_lags(df, use or names)
    return df["spx"].loc[X.index].values, X.values


def test_betas_agree_with_numpy_and_with_each_other(spx):
    b = factors.betas(spx, ["copper", "dollar"])
    df = factors.table(spx, ["copper", "dollar"])
    for n in ("copper", "dollar"):
        c = np.corrcoef(df["spx"], df[n])[0, 1]
        assert b[n]["corr"] == pytest.approx(c)
        assert b[n]["spx_beta"] == pytest.approx(np.polyfit(df[n], df["spx"], 1)[0])
        assert b[n]["spx_beta"] * b[n]["factor_beta"] == pytest.approx(c ** 2)   # the two slopes multiply to r^2
    assert b["dollar"]["corr"] < 0 < b["copper"]["corr"]


# --------------------------------------------------------------- rolling / crash corr
def test_rolling_corr_of_a_series_with_its_multiple():
    days = pd.bdate_range("2000-01-03", periods=600)
    a = pd.Series(np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=600), index=days)
    assert factors.rolling_corr(a, 2 * a, 50).values == pytest.approx(1)
    assert factors.rolling_corr(a, -a, 50).values == pytest.approx(-1)
    assert len(factors.rolling_corr(a, a, 50)) == 600 - 49
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="window"):
        factors.rolling_corr(a, a, 2)


def test_crash_corr_sees_a_link_that_exists_only_in_crashes():
    g = np.random.default_rng(1)
    days = pd.bdate_range("2000-01-03", periods=4000)
    r = pd.Series(g.normal(size=4000), index=days)
    f = pd.Series(g.normal(size=4000), index=days)
    worst = r <= r.quantile(0.05)
    f[worst] = r[worst]                       # moves exactly with the S&P, but only on its worst days
    on_worst, other = factors.crash_corr(r, f.rename("f"))
    assert on_worst == pytest.approx(1)
    assert abs(other) < 0.05


# --------------------------------------------------------------- on_days / event_days
def test_on_days_maps_holidays_to_the_next_trading_day():
    idx = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2020-03-12", "2020-03-13", "2020-03-16", "2020-03-17"])
    m = factors.on_days(idx, ["2020-03-15", "2020-03-12", "2020-03-20"])   # Sunday, Thursday, after the end
    assert m.tolist() == [True, False, True, False]
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="sorted"):
        factors.on_days(idx[::-1], ["2020-03-12"])


def test_event_days_on_the_biggest_days():
    g = np.random.default_rng(2)
    r = pd.Series(g.standard_t(3, 10_000))
    a = np.abs(r - r.mean())
    mask = (a >= np.quantile(a, 0.99)).values                # exactly the biggest 1%

"""Tests for herding/factors.py, the outside-factor data files, the Fed decision days, and
scripts/outside_news_figures.py (Figs 16-18).

Every test states what "correct" means and checks it against an answer found another way:
made-up data with a known answer (an exact line, a mirror image), a property least squares
must have (residuals uncorrelated with every regressor), or a published historical fact.
"""
import importlib.util

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest
from matplotlib.image import imread

from conftest import ROOT, SEEDS
from herding import factors, market_data, stats


def downloader():
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("download", ROOT / "data/download_market_data.py")
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
    return mod


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def spx():
    return market_data.spx_returns()


# --------------------------------------------------------------- data files
# Spec: each file is clean, ends on the project's fixed day, and matches known history.

def test_factor_files_are_clean_and_end_on_the_fixed_day():
    end = pd.Timestamp(downloader().END)
    for name, f in factors.FACTORS.items():
        prices = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / f)        # checks sorted, unique, > 0
        assert prices.index[-1] <= end, name
        assert (end - prices.index[-1]).days <= 4, name                 # at most a long weekend early


def test_brent_known_prices():
    # EIA: Brent's record close was $143.95 on 2008-07-03; it fell to $9.12 on 2020-04-21
    brent = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "oil_brent.csv")["Close"]
    assert brent["2008-07-03"] == pytest.approx(143.95)
    assert brent.idxmax() == pd.Timestamp("2008-07-03")
    assert brent["2020-04-21"] == pytest.approx(9.12)


def test_ten_year_yield_known_values():
    # The 10-year yield's all-time high was 15.84% (1981-09-30); it fell 0.75 points the
    # day after Black Monday as money fled to bonds
    y = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "treasury_10y_yield.csv")["Close"]
    assert y.idxmax() == pd.Timestamp("1981-09-30") and y.max() == pytest.approx(15.84)
    assert factors.changes("rates")["1987-10-20"] == pytest.approx(-0.75)


def test_fed_target_known_moves():
    # Fed history: cut to a 0-0.25% range on 2008-12-16; to 0-0.25% again on 2020-03-15
    t = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "fed_funds_target.csv")["Close"]
    assert t["2008-12-15"] == pytest.approx(1.0) and t["2008-12-16"] == pytest.approx(0.25)
    assert t["2020-03-16"] == pytest.approx(0.25) and t["2020-03-13"] == pytest.approx(1.25)


# --------------------------------------------------------------- Fed decision days
def test_surprise_moves_are_exactly_the_feds_intermeeting_moves():
    # The Fed's moves between scheduled meetings since 1994 (federalreserve.gov, "Open market
    # operations" history), dated by announcement, typed in here by hand
    known = {"1994-04-18": 25, "1998-10-15": -25, "2001-01-03": -50, "2001-04-18": -50,
             "2001-09-17": -50, "2008-01-22": -75, "2008-10-08": -50, "2020-03-03": -50,
             "2020-03-15": -100}
    d = factors.decisions("unscheduled")
    assert dict(zip(d["date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"), d["change_bp"])) == known


def test_scheduled_meetings_known_decisions():
    d = factors.decisions("scheduled").set_index("date")["change_bp"]
    assert d["2008-12-16"] == -75             # 1.00% -> 0-0.25%
    assert d["2022-06-15"] == 75              # the first 0.75-point hike since 1994
    assert d["2023-09-20"] == 0               # a pause
    assert d["2006-01-31"] == 25


def test_scheduled_meetings_are_weekdays_and_about_eight_a_year():
    d = factors.decisions("scheduled")["date"]
    assert (d.dt.dayofweek < 5).all()
    per_year = d.groupby(d.dt.year).size()
    assert per_year.between(7, 9).all(), per_year[~per_year.between(7, 9)]
    assert d.is_unique


def test_every_target_change_is_assigned_to_exactly_one_decision():
    # The changes in the target series must add up to the changes in the decision file
    t = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "fed_funds_target.csv")["Close"]
    t = t[t.index >= "1994-01-01"]
    total = round((t.iloc[-1] - t.iloc[0]) * 100)
    assert factors.decisions()["change_bp"].sum() == total


def test_decisions_rejects_unknown_kind():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="kind"):
        factors.decisions("emergency")


# The rules that build fed_decisions.csv, on made-up targets and meetings
@pytest.fixture
def dm(monkeypatch):
    mod = downloader()
    monkeypatch.setattr(mod, "scheduled_fomc_days",
                        lambda: pd.DatetimeIndex(["2005-03-22", "2005-05-03", "2015-12-16", "2016-03-16"]))
    return mod


def target(changes):
    days = pd.bdate_range("2005-01-03", "2016-06-30")
    rate = pd.Series(1.0, index=days)
    for day, bp in changes:
        rate[rate.index >= day] += bp / 100
    return rate.rename("Close").to_frame()


def test_fed_decisions_same_day_change_before_2008(dm):
    d = dm.fed_decisions(target([("2005-03-22", 25)]))
    assert d.set_index("date").loc["2005-03-22", "change_bp"] == 25
    assert (d["kind"] == "unscheduled").sum() == 0


def test_fed_decisions_next_day_change_after_2008_belongs_to_the_meeting(dm):
    # Since 2008-12-16 a new range takes effect the day after the announcement
    d = dm.fed_decisions(target([("2015-12-17", 25)]))
    assert d.set_index("date").loc["2015-12-16", "change_bp"] == 25
    assert (d["kind"] == "unscheduled").sum() == 0


def test_fed_decisions_surprise_is_dated_by_its_announcement(dm):
    d = dm.fed_decisions(target([("2005-04-12", -50), ("2016-01-20", -25)]))
    s = d[d["kind"] == "unscheduled"].set_index("date")["change_bp"]
    assert s.to_dict() == {pd.Timestamp("2005-04-12"): -50, pd.Timestamp("2016-01-19"): -25}


def test_last_day_of_meeting_parsing():
    mod = downloader()
    assert mod._last_day("March", "17-18", 2026) == pd.Timestamp("2026-03-18")
    assert mod._last_day("Oct/Nov", "31-1", 2023) == pd.Timestamp("2023-11-01")
    assert mod._last_day("September", "20", 2005) == pd.Timestamp("2005-09-20")


# --------------------------------------------------------------- changes / table
def test_changes_are_log_changes_or_yield_differences():
    oil = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "oil_brent.csv")["Close"]
    assert factors.changes("oil")["2020-04-21"] == pytest.approx(np.log(9.12 / 17.36))
    y = market_data.load_prices(factors.FACTOR_DIR / "treasury_10y_yield.csv")["Close"]
    assert factors.changes("rates").values == pytest.approx(np.diff(y.values))
    assert len(factors.changes("oil")) == len(oil) - 1


def test_changes_rejects_unknown_factor():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="unknown factor"):
        factors.changes("silver")


def test_table_keeps_only_days_every_series_has(spx):
    df = factors.table(spx, ["oil", "dollar"])
    assert not df.isna().any().any()
    assert df.index.isin(spx.index).all()
    assert df.index.isin(factors.changes("dollar").index).all()
    assert df.index[0] >= pd.Timestamp("2006-01-03")          # the dollar series starts in 2006


def test_table_needs_factors_and_enough_days(spx):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="at least one"):
        factors.table(spx, [])
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="500"):
        factors.table(spx.iloc[-300:], ["oil"])


# --------------------------------------------------------------- with_leads_lags
def test_leads_and_lags_shift_the_right_way():
    df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, 2, 3, 4, 5]}, index=pd.bdate_range("2020-01-06", periods=5))
    out = factors.with_leads_lags(df, ["x"], 1)
    assert list(out.columns) == ["x[-1]", "x[+0]", "x[+1]"]
    assert out["x[-1]"].tolist() == [1, 2, 3]       # yesterday
    assert out["x[+0]"].tolist() == [2, 3, 4]
    assert out["x[+1]"].tolist() == [3, 4, 5]       # tomorrow
    assert factors.with_leads_lags(df, ["x"], 0)["x[+0]"].tolist() == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("bad", [-1, 1.5, True])
def test_leads_and_lags_rejects_bad_lags(bad):
    df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, 2, 3]})
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="lags"):
        factors.with_leads_lags(df, ["x"], bad)


# --------------------------------------------------------------- regress
@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_regress_recovers_an_exact_line(seed):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = g.normal(size=(200, 2))
    beta, icept, r2, resid = factors.regress(2 + 3 * X[:, 0] - X[:, 1], X)
    assert beta == pytest.approx([3, -1]) and icept == pytest.approx(2)
    assert r2 == pytest.approx(1) and np.abs(resid).max() < 1e-10


@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_regress_r2_matches_the_signal_share(seed):
    # y = x + noise with equal variances: R^2 should be about 1/2
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = g.normal(size=200_000)
    _, _, r2, resid = factors.regress(x + g.normal(size=x.size), x)
    assert r2 == pytest.approx(0.5, abs=0.01)
    assert abs(np.corrcoef(resid, x)[0, 1]) < 1e-10          # least squares: residual _|_ regressor


def test_regress_rejects_bad_input():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="constant"):
        factors.regress(np.ones(10), np.arange(10.0))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="one row"):
        factors.regress(np.arange(10.0), np.arange(9.0))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="more rows"):
        factors.regress(np.arange(3.0), np.ones((3, 2)))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="NaN"):
        factors.regress(np.arange(5.0), np.array([1, 2, np.nan, 4, 5]))


# --------------------------------------------------------------- remove / betas
def test_remove_leaves_nothing_the_factors_can_explain(spx):
    names = ["oil", "rates"]
    resid, r2 = factors.remove(spx, names)
    X = factors.with_leads_lags(factors.table(spx, names), names).loc[resid.index]
    for col in X:
        assert abs(np.corrcoef(resid, X[col])[0, 1]) < 1e-8, col
    assert resid.mean() == pytest.approx(spx.loc[resid.index].mean())
    assert 0 < r2 < 1


def test_more_factors_never_explain_less(spx):
    # Nested least squares: adding regressors can only raise R^2 (on the same days)
    small = factors.regress(*_design(spx, ["oil", "gold", "copper", "dollar", "rates"], ["oil"]))[2]
    big = factors.regress(*_design(spx, ["oil", "gold", "copper", "dollar", "rates"]))[2]
    assert big >= small


def _design(spx, names, use=None):
    df = factors.table(spx, names)
    X = factors.with_leads_lags(df, use or names)
    return df["spx"].loc[X.index].values, X.values


def test_betas_agree_with_numpy_and_with_each_other(spx):
    b = factors.betas(spx, ["copper", "dollar"])
    df = factors.table(spx, ["copper", "dollar"])
    for n in ("copper", "dollar"):
        c = np.corrcoef(df["spx"], df[n])[0, 1]
        assert b[n]["corr"] == pytest.approx(c)
        assert b[n]["spx_beta"] == pytest.approx(np.polyfit(df[n], df["spx"], 1)[0])
        assert b[n]["spx_beta"] * b[n]["factor_beta"] == pytest.approx(c ** 2)   # the two slopes multiply to r^2
    assert b["dollar"]["corr"] < 0 < b["copper"]["corr"]


# --------------------------------------------------------------- rolling / crash corr
def test_rolling_corr_of_a_series_with_its_multiple():
    days = pd.bdate_range("2000-01-03", periods=600)
    a = pd.Series(np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=600), index=days)
    assert factors.rolling_corr(a, 2 * a, 50).values == pytest.approx(1)
    assert factors.rolling_corr(a, -a, 50).values == pytest.approx(-1)
    assert len(factors.rolling_corr(a, a, 50)) == 600 - 49
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="window"):
        factors.rolling_corr(a, a, 2)


def test_crash_corr_sees_a_link_that_exists_only_in_crashes():
    g = np.random.default_rng(1)
    days = pd.bdate_range("2000-01-03", periods=4000)
    r = pd.Series(g.normal(size=4000), index=days)
    f = pd.Series(g.normal(size=4000), index=days)
    worst = r <= r.quantile(0.05)
    f[worst] = r[worst]                       # moves exactly with the S&P, but only on its worst days
    on_worst, other = factors.crash_corr(r, f.rename("f"))
    assert on_worst == pytest.approx(1)
    assert abs(other) < 0.05


# --------------------------------------------------------------- on_days / event_days
def test_on_days_maps_holidays_to_the_next_trading_day():
    idx = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2020-03-12", "2020-03-13", "2020-03-16", "2020-03-17"])
    m = factors.on_days(idx, ["2020-03-15", "2020-03-12", "2020-03-20"])   # Sunday, Thursday, after the end
    assert m.tolist() == [True, False, True, False]
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="sorted"):
        factors.on_days(idx[::-1], ["2020-03-12"])


def test_event_days_on_the_biggest_days():
    g = np.random.default_rng(2)
    r = pd.Series(g.standard_t(3, 10_000))
    a = np.abs(r - r.mean())

def test_event_days_rejects_bad_masks():
    r = pd.Series(np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=100))
    for bad in (np.zeros(100, bool), np.ones(100, bool)):

            factors.event_days(r, bad)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="one True/False"):
        factors.event_days(r, np.zeros(99, bool))


def test_r2_by_regime_is_three_shares(spx):
    out = factors.r2_by_regime(spx, ["oil", "copper"])
    assert list(out) == ["calm", "middle", "wild"]
    assert all(0 <= v <= 1 for v in out.values())

    import outside_news_figures as onf
    from multiprocessing import Pool
    onf.plots.style()
    f16 = onf.fig16_comovement(spx, tmp_path / "16.png")

# --------------------------------------------------------------- skewness, block_indices, moments
# Spec: skewness is 0 for symmetric data, 2 for an exponential distribution, and flips sign
# in a mirror; block_indices gives n positions in runs of consecutive days; moments gives the
# four plain moments with intervals that contain them.

@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_skewness_known_values(seed):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    e = g.exponential(size=400_000)
    assert stats.skewness(e) == pytest.approx(2, abs=0.05)          # exponential: skewness 2
    assert stats.skewness(-e) == pytest.approx(-stats.skewness(e))  # the mirror image
    assert abs(stats.skewness(g.normal(size=400_000))) < 0.02
    assert stats.skewness([1.0, 2, 3]) == 0


def test_skewness_rejects_constant_input():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="constant"):
        stats.skewness([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])


@pytest.mark.parametrize("wrap", [True, False])
def test_block_indices_are_runs_of_consecutive_days(wrap):
    g = np.random.default_rng(0)
    i = stats.block_indices(103, 10, g, wrap)
    assert len(i) == 103 and i.min() >= 0 and i.max() < 103
    for run in np.split(i, range(10, 103, 10)):
        steps = np.diff(run) % 103 if wrap else np.diff(run)
        assert (steps == 1).all()


def test_block_indices_without_wrap_never_runs_past_the_end():
    g = np.random.default_rng(3)
    for _ in range(200):
        i = stats.block_indices(50, 49, g, wrap=False)
        assert (np.diff(i[:49]) == 1).all() and i.max() < 50


@pytest.mark.parametrize("bad", [0, 11, 2.5, True])
def test_block_indices_rejects_bad_blocks(bad):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="block"):
        stats.block_indices(10, bad, np.random.default_rng(0))


def test_moments_are_the_plain_moments_with_intervals_around_them():
    r = np.random.default_rng(4).standard_t(5, 5000) * 0.01
    m = stats.moments(r, block=20, draws=300)
    assert m["mean"][0] == pytest.approx(r.mean()) and m["sd"][0] == pytest.approx(r.std())
    assert m["skew"][0] == pytest.approx(stats.skewness(r)) and m["kurtosis"][0] == pytest.approx(stats.kurtosis(r))
    for v, lo, hi in m.values():
        assert lo <= v <= hi


def test_moments_interval_has_the_textbook_width_for_white_noise():
    # For n independent bell-curve days, the mean's 95% interval is about +-1.96 sd / sqrt(n)
    n = 10_000
    r = np.random.default_rng(5).normal(size=n)
    _, lo, hi = stats.moments(r, block=1, draws=2000)["mean"]
    assert (hi - lo) / 2 == pytest.approx(1.96 / np.sqrt(n), rel=0.1)


def test_moments_rejects_bad_draws():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="draws"):
        stats.moments(np.arange(10.0), draws=1)

def test_block_indices_rejects_bad_blocks(bad):

def test_moments_are_the_plain_moments_with_intervals_around_them():

    m = stats.moments(r, block=20, draws=300)
    assert m["mean"][0] == pytest.approx(r.mean()) and m["sd"][0] == pytest.approx(r.std())
    assert m["skew"][0] == pytest.approx(stats.skewness(r)) and m["kurtosis"][0] == pytest.approx(stats.kurtosis(r))
    for v, lo, hi in m.values():
        assert lo <= v <= hi


def test_moments_interval_has_the_textbook_width_for_white_noise():
    # For n independent bell-curve days, the mean's 95% interval is about +-1.96 sd / sqrt(n)
    n = 10_000
    r = np.random.default_rng(5).normal(size=n)
    _, lo, hi = stats.moments(r, block=1, draws=2000)["mean"]
    assert (hi - lo) / 2 == pytest.approx(1.96 / np.sqrt(n), rel=0.1)
